title: What Is an Abstract Data Type?
summary: The distinction between an Abstract Data Type — what operations a structure supports — and a data structure — how it's actually built in memory to support them.

references.label: Sedgewick & Wayne — Algorithms, Part I (Princeton, Coursera)

title: Static Arrays and Random Access
summary: A fixed-size, contiguous block of memory that supports O(1) access to any element by index — and why that contiguity is exactly what makes random access fast.

title: Dynamic Arrays and Amortized Resizing
summary: An array that grows by doubling its capacity when full — and why that doubling strategy makes appending an element O(1) on average (amortized), even though any single append can be O(n).

references.label: Sedgewick & Wayne — Stacks and Queues (Princeton lecture slides)

title: Singly Linked Lists
summary: A sequence built from nodes scattered anywhere in memory, each pointing to the next — trading array's O(1) random access for O(1) insertion at a known position.

title: Doubly Linked Lists
summary: A linked list whose nodes also point backward, enabling O(1) removal of a known node and O(1) traversal in either direction, at the cost of an extra pointer per node.

title: Arrays vs. Linked Lists: Choosing a Sequence
summary: Neither structure dominates the other — a side-by-side comparison of access, insertion, deletion, and memory locality to decide which sequence fits a given problem.

references.label: Sedgewick & Wayne — Algorithms, Part I (Princeton, Coursera)

title: The Stack ADT (LIFO)
summary: A Last-In-First-Out structure exposing only push and pop — and how the same ADT can be implemented equally well atop a resizing array or a linked list.

references.label: Sedgewick & Wayne — Stacks and Queues (Princeton lecture slides)

title: The Queue ADT (FIFO)
summary: A First-In-First-Out structure exposing enqueue and dequeue — and why a naive array implementation needs a circular buffer to keep both operations O(1).

references.label: Sedgewick & Wayne — Stacks and Queues (Princeton lecture slides)

title: Deques
summary: A double-ended queue supporting O(1) insertion and removal at both ends — a strict generalization that subsumes both the stack and the queue.

references.label: Sedgewick & Wayne — Stacks and Queues (Princeton lecture slides)

title: Iterators: Traversing a Collection Uniformly
summary: A uniform way to walk through any collection's elements one at a time without exposing how that collection is actually stored underneath.

references.label: Sedgewick & Wayne — Stacks and Queues (Princeton lecture slides)
Sedgewick & Wayne — Algorithms, Part I (Princeton, Coursera)

title: Hashing and Hash Functions
summary: Mapping a key to an array index via a hash function, aiming for near-constant-time lookup — and the properties (determinism, uniformity) a good hash function needs.

references.label: Sedgewick & Wayne — Algorithms, Part I (Princeton, Coursera)

title: Collision Resolution: Separate Chaining
summary: Resolving two keys that hash to the same index by storing a small list at each array slot — simple to implement, degrading gracefully as collisions accumulate.

references.label: Sedgewick & Wayne — Algorithms, Part I (Princeton, Coursera)

title: Collision Resolution: Open Addressing
summary: Resolving a collision by probing for the next open slot in the array itself, rather than chaining elsewhere — and the clustering problems that come with it.

references.label: Sedgewick & Wayne — Algorithms, Part I (Princeton, Coursera)

title: Load Factor and Rehashing
summary: The ratio of stored elements to table capacity, and why a hash table must resize (rehash) once that ratio grows too large to keep operations close to O(1).

references.label: Sedgewick & Wayne — Algorithms, Part I (Princeton, Coursera)

title: Binary Trees: Terminology and Representation
summary: A tree where every node has at most two children — how the graph-theoretic tree from discrete math becomes a concrete node-and-pointer data structure.

title: Tree Traversals: Preorder, Inorder, Postorder, Level-Order
summary: Four standard orders for visiting every node in a binary tree exactly once — three defined recursively, one defined by processing level by level with a queue.

title: Binary Search Trees: Search, Insert, Delete
summary: A binary tree with an ordering invariant — everything in a node's left subtree is smaller, everything in its right subtree is larger — that turns search into following one path from the root.

references.label: Sedgewick & Wayne — Algorithms, Part I (Princeton, Coursera)

title: BST Performance: Why Balance Matters
summary: A binary search tree's operations are O(log n) on average but degrade to O(n) on a lopsided tree — the exact problem that motivates the self-balancing trees covered later, in Data Structures II.

references.label: Sedgewick & Wayne — Algorithms, Part I (Princeton, Coursera)
